title: A Land That Drinks the Rain: Blessing and Curse
summary: Moses reminds the adults before him that they, not their children, saw God's mighty acts in Egypt and the wilderness, and he calls them to love and obey God. Canaan, unlike Egypt, depends on rain from heaven, and God promises rain in season for faithfulness and drought for idolatry. Moses repeats the call to keep God's words on heart, hand, and doorpost, and he sets before Israel a blessing and a curse, to be proclaimed on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal once they enter the land.
story: Chapter 11 closes the long appeal that began in chapter 6, and it gathers that appeal's main themes: love for God, memory of what he has done, teaching the children, and the danger of other gods. It also points ahead. The blessing and the curse set before Israel here (verses 26 to 28) will be spelled out in detail in chapters 27 and 28, and the ceremony at Gerizim and Ebal is carried out in Joshua 8:30-35. With this chapter the sermon ends and the law code begins; chapter 12 opens the detailed statutes and ordinances. Moses has argued for loyalty at length before listing its terms, because the laws only make sense to a people who love the God who gives them.
historical:
Moses recalls two kinds of events: God's acts against Egypt, including the drowning of Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea (Exodus 14), and his judgment inside Israel on Dathan and Abiram, who rebelled against Moses' leadership and were swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16). The generation standing before him had been young then, which is why he insists that their own eyes saw these things (verse 7).

Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal stand on either side of the valley at Shechem, near modern Nablus, in the central hill country; the Oak of Moreh (verse 30) was near Shechem, where God first appeared to Abraham in the land (Genesis 12:6-7). Gerizim later became the holy mountain of the Samaritans, who built a temple there, and the woman at the well in John 4 refers to it. On Mount Ebal, the Israeli archaeologist Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure in the 1980s that he identified as an early Israelite altar; others read it as a farmstead or watchtower, and the question remains debated. The borders in verse 24, from the wilderness to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean, describe the full extent of the promise; Israel's control came closest to them under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21).
cultural:
Verses 10 to 12 contrast two kinds of farming. Egypt's agriculture depended on the Nile's yearly flood and on irrigation channels, which farmers managed by hand and foot, opening and closing small earthen dams or working water-lifting devices. Canaan had no great river; its farms depended on rain, which came in two seasons: the autumn rains that softened the ground for plowing and sowing, and the spring rains that brought the grain to harvest. A failure of either could mean famine. That made rain a matter of life and death, and it is why the Canaanite storm god Baal, believed to bring the rain, was such a powerful temptation to Israel. Moses insists that the rain comes from the LORD, whose eyes are on the land all year.

The ceremony of blessing and curse on two mountains fits ancient covenant practice, in which treaties ended with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal and were sometimes solemnized in public. Setting them on two facing mountains made the choice visible to the whole people gathered in the valley between.
literary: The chapter is built from exhortations, each opened with a call to keep God's commands (verses 1, 8, 13, 22) and each followed by a reason or a promise. Verses 18 to 21 repeat almost word for word the instructions of 6:6-9, forming a bracket around the whole sermon of chapters 6 to 11. The chapter ends with a clear either-or, "a blessing and a curse" (verse 26), set out in balanced parallel lines (verses 27 and 28), a structure that anticipates the covenant ceremony of chapters 27 and 28 and the final choice between life and death in chapter 30.

outline.t: Your own eyes have seen what God did
A land that drinks the rain from heaven
Keep these words on heart, hand, and doorpost
The promise of the land for the faithful
Blessing and curse, Gerizim and Ebal

doctrines.note: The land's fertility depends on God's care: "the eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year" (verse 12). Rain, harvest, and pasture are not the gifts of a storm god or the product of human effort alone, but the ongoing work of the LORD.

The covenant carries real consequences. Faithfulness brings blessing and betrayal brings curse, and Israel is set before that choice with open eyes. The blessings are God's gifts within a relationship, not payments for services.

The command to teach God's words to children, sitting at home and walking along the road, is repeated from chapter 6. Moses addresses the generation who saw God's works and makes them responsible for passing that memory to those who did not.

words.note: Matar, rain. In verses 11, 14, and 17 rain is the hinge of Israel's life in the land. The chapter names the two seasonal rains separately, the autumn and the spring rains, and presents both as the LORD's gift. Withholding rain is one of the covenant curses, as Elijah's drought in 1 Kings 17 later shows.

Berakhah, blessing. In the Old Testament a blessing is not only good wishes but God's active favor that brings life, fruitfulness, and flourishing. It goes back to God's first words to humanity in Genesis 1:28 and to his promise to bless Abraham and all nations through him (Genesis 12:2-3).

Qelalah, curse. The opposite of blessing: God's favor withdrawn and the powers of life turned against a person or people. In covenant language the curse is the penalty the covenant partner accepts for breaking faith.

christ: Jesus taught that the Father "sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous" (Matthew 5:45), a reminder that rain is always God's gift, even to those who do not honor him. The chapter's choice between blessing and curse becomes central to Paul's argument in Galatians 3, where he says "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). In Christian teaching, Christ bore the curse that covenant-breakers deserved so that the blessing promised to Abraham could reach the nations. When the Samaritan woman at the well spoke of worship on Mount Gerizim, Jesus told her that the time was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth rather than on one mountain or another (John 4:20-24).

hard.q: Does this chapter promise that faithful people will always prosper and that hardship is always punishment?
hard.a:
Verses 13 to 17 link Israel's obedience to rain and harvest and their idolatry to drought. Some have read passages like this as a guarantee that faith brings wealth and health to individuals, the claim at the center of prosperity teaching. Most interpreters across Jewish and Christian traditions reject that reading. The promises are made to the nation of Israel within a particular covenant tied to a particular land, and they describe the covenant's shape over time rather than a formula for each person's circumstances. The rest of the Old Testament itself pushes back against a mechanical reading: Job suffers though righteous, and several psalms and the book of Ecclesiastes complain that the wicked often prosper. Jesus rejected the assumption that suffering proves sin (John 9:1-3; Luke 13:1-5).

At the same time, the chapter should not be emptied of meaning. It teaches that the world belongs to God, that faithfulness and unfaithfulness matter, and that a people's relationship with God affects their life together. Christians read its promises through Christ, in whom the deepest blessings are spiritual and eternal, and who himself suffered though righteous.

questions: Moses stresses that the people had seen God's works with their own eyes. What have you seen God do that you need to pass on to people who did not see it?
Israel's life depended on rain they could not control. What in your life reminds you that you depend on God for what you cannot produce yourself?
The chapter sets a blessing and a curse before Israel as a real choice. What choices in front of you now carry more weight than they first appear?
